rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyone should reflect on their deeds and assess how they will fare on the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: everyone should reflect upon their deeds and evaluate how they may fare on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Seeing some Muslims in poverty, the Prophet gathered people and recited 4:1 followed by this verse; many then brought food and clothing for the poor.
rows.anchor: It is reported that upon seeing the impoverished state of some Muslims, the Prophet called the people together and then recited 4:1

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Madinan sūrah takes its name from hypocrites who affirmed Muhammad’s prophethood and fealty while continuing to ally with his enemies.
rows.anchor: discussion of the hypocrites who attested to the prophethood of Muhammad and swore fealty to him, but continued to ally themselves with his enemies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Munāfiqūn contrasts with al-Jumuʿah, which addresses believers.
rows.anchor: a contrast to the previous sūrah, al-Jumuʿah, which addresses the believers

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet frequently recited al-Jumuʿah in Friday prayer’s first cycle to encourage believers and al-Munāfiqūn in the second as a rebuke to hypocrites.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have frequently recited these two sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of the sūrah warns about the hypocrites’ treachery.
rows.anchor: Most of the sūrah warns of the treachery of the hypocrites (vv. 1–8)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final verses command believers not to let worldly responsibilities and desires distract them from remembering God, paralleling 62:9–11.
rows.anchor: the final verses of this sūrah (vv. 9–11) enjoin the believers not to allow the responsibilities and desires of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s placement warns that subtler forms of hypocrisy can distract believers from fulfilling religious duties.
rows.anchor: a reminder of the more subtle forms of hypocrisy that can distract those who believe from the proper fulfillment of their religious obligations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children do not bring people near to God apart from faith and righteous action; enduring righteous deeds are better than worldly adornments.
rows.anchor: Wealth or your children that bring you nigh in nearness unto Us, save those who believe and work righteousness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Judgment Day, wealth and children avail nothing except for the one who comes to God with a sound heart.
rows.anchor: the Day of Judgment is thus described as the Day when neither wealth nor children avail, save for him who comes to God with a sound heart

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deal justly with worldly possessions and responsibilities are rewarded, while wealth and children cannot protect disbelievers from God.
rows.anchor: Those who meet the challenge, dealing justly with their worldly possessions and responsibilities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran warns that God may punish disbelievers through their wealth and children in this life, and cites other warnings about worldly attachments.
rows.anchor: God desires but to punish them thereby in the life of this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Remembrance of God” can mean the practice of dhikr, remembrance of God.
rows.anchor: As rendered, the remembrance of God refers to the practice of ḍhikr or remembrance of God

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: An alternative rendering is “the reminder of God,” referring to the Quran because Reminder is one of the Quran’s names.
rows.anchor: It could also be rendered “the reminder of God,” in which case it would refer to the Quran (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: These verses indicate that zakāh should be paid promptly and obligatory religious duties should not be delayed.
rows.anchor: These verses are understood to indicate the need to pay the zakāh (alms) with dispatch; likewise, there should be no delay in performing any

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: At death, anyone who fell short in paying zakāh will ask to return to this world, apparently to make up the missed payment.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn ʿAbbās, “Every person who has fallen short in [paying] zakāh will ask to be returned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a person’s appointed term comes, death arrives and the door of repentance closes.
rows.anchor: When its term has come refers to the moment of death, at which point the door of repentance is closed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning follows the sūrah’s theme of hypocrisy: although sincere repentance is possible before death, one should not deliberately wait until death to repent.
rows.anchor: Although every soul is granted reprieve until the moment of death to make sincere repentance, from a Quranic perspective one should not make a calculated decision to wait

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God grants every soul time to repent out of mercy and forgiveness; otherwise, human beings would be wiped from the earth for their deeds.
rows.anchor: everyone is granted reprieve out of God’s Mercy and Forgiveness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deliberately postpone repentance and good deeds until death receive no reprieve once their term arrives.
rows.anchor: those who deliberately wait until the moment of death to repent and perform good deeds are granted no reprieve

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most classify the sūrah as Madinan, while some consider it Makkan.
rows.anchor: considered by most to be Madinan, and by some to be Makkan

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: A saying attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās holds that the whole sūrah was revealed in Makkah except its last verse.
rows.anchor: According to a saying attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, the entire sūrah was revealed in Makkah except the last verse

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Another reported view is that every verse except 14–16 is Makkan.
rows.anchor: Others are said to have maintained that all but vv. 14–16 are Makkan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s title comes from its unique description of the Judgment Day as the Day of Mutual Dispossession.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the reference to the Day of Judgment as the Day of Mutual Dispossession in v. 9, a concept unique to the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the last of the “Glorifiers,” sūrahs that begin by mentioning God’s glorification; the others are 57, 59, 61, and 62.
rows.anchor: which begin with a reference to the glorification of God; the other “Glorifiers” are 57, 59, 61, and 62

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where the previous sūrah distinguishes hypocrites from believers and calls hypocrites to repent, this one distinguishes believers from disbelievers and warns the latter of their fate.
rows.anchor: the previous sūrah distinguishes between the hypocrites and the believers, calling upon the hypocrites to repent, so too does this sūrah distinguish between the believers and the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both sūrahs end by warning that property and children can distract or test people and urging spending in God’s way before death.
rows.anchor: Both sūrah s end with a warning that property and children can be a source of diversion and thus of trial (63:9; 64:15) and with a reminder to spend in the way of God before being overcome by death (63:10; 64:16)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of Gathering is Resurrection, when all people across generations and all jinn assemble on a barren plain for judgment, each community behind its prophet, and all living things ultimately gather to their Lord.
rows.anchor: all human beings of all generations and all jinn will be gathered on a single open, barren plain for judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may also refer to God gathering people’s bones to resurrect them, answering disbelievers who object that bones and dust cannot become a new creation.
rows.anchor: It can also be seen as a reference to God’s gathering together one’s bones for resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taghābun derives from ghabana, “to stint or shortchange another in a transaction,” with an implication of deception or subterfuge.
rows.anchor: Mutual Dispossession renders taghābun, which derives from ghabana, meaning “to stint or shortchange another in a transaction”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term most likely refers to Resurrection because humans cannot fully repay God for what He has done, even though every soul is paid fully for its own deeds.
rows.anchor: there is no way that human beings can fully repay the debt they owe to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are described as selling their souls for God’s pleasure and exchanging worldly life for the Hereafter; God purchases their souls and wealth for the Garden in a one-sided transaction.
rows.anchor: one could be said to have “stinted”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who sell God’s covenant and oaths for a small price shortchange themselves; they have traded guidance for error and will not be rightly guided.
rows.anchor: those who sell God’s pact and their oaths for a paltry price (3:77) have stinted or shortchanged themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By contrast, those who sell their souls for God have their sins absolved in this life and enter Paradise in the next; attaining the Garden is called the great triumph.
rows.anchor: those who sell their souls for God have their evil deeds absolved in this life and enter Paradise in the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of entering Gardens with rivers running below is discussed in relation to several other verses.
rows.anchor: Regarding God’s admitting people into Gardens with rivers running below

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Madinan sūrah is named for its divorce guidelines and is also called “The Shorter Sūrah Regarding Women,” in contrast with Sūrah 4.
rows.anchor: Al-Ṭalāq is a Madinan sūrah that takes its name from the guidelines it provides for divorce

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A hadith says that, among permitted things, divorce is the most abhorred by God.
rows.anchor: A ḥadīth states, “Verily, of that which is permitted, the most abhorred by God is divorce.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet himself is permitted to divorce his wives in 33:28–29.
rows.anchor: in 33:28–29 the Prophet himself is permitted to divorce his wives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first section details divorce waiting periods and a husband’s support obligations, especially for pregnant or nursing wives; verses 8–12 remind Muslims to obey the laws by recalling earlier peoples who failed to do so.
rows.anchor: The first (vv. 1–7) provides details regarding the waiting period to be observed in cases of divorce

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some interpret the husband’s payment to his former wife as depending on both her needs and his circumstances.
rows.anchor: Some interpret this verse to mean that the amount paid by the husband to his former wife depends upon both her needs and his circumstances

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say the amount paid to the former wife should be limited to her immediate needs.
rows.anchor: others maintain that the amount the wife must be paid is to be limited to her immediate needs

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The verse is also taken as evidence that the husband alone must provide for the child, whether the couple remains married or is divorced.
rows.anchor: This verse is also viewed as evidence for the position that the husband is solely responsible for providing provisions for the child

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If these obligations are difficult, God will ease circumstances either by providing means in this life or by easing one’s way into the Garden for observing His command despite hardship.
rows.anchor: God will ease one’s circumstances, either in this life by providing additional means or in the Hereafter by easing one’s way into the Garden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qalam is generally considered an early Makkan sūrah.
rows.anchor: generally thought to be from the early Makkan period

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Qatādah
rows.claim: These early commentators held that verses 1–16, 34–47, and 51–52 are Makkan, while 17–33 and 48–50 are Madinan.
rows.anchor: the early commentators IbnʿAbbās and al-Qatādah (d. 117/726) maintained that vv. 1–16

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from the pen mentioned in its first verse.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the mention of the pen in the first verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening section contrasts believers and disbelievers, whose true nature many disbelievers will recognize only at Resurrection and Judgment.
rows.anchor: The first section of the sūrah (vv. 1–10) contrasts the natures of those who believe and those who disbelieve

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 11–16 warn believers not to follow people of base character merely because of their worldly wealth.
rows.anchor: cautioning the believers not to follow people of base character simply because of their worldly wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 17–34 tell the parable of garden owners who lose their harvest because of miserliness.
rows.anchor: the parable of the owners of the garden, who lost their harvest because of their miserliness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 35–47 return to the believer-disbeliever contrast and expose the emptiness of the disbelievers’ position through rhetorical questions.
rows.anchor: returns to the contrast of the believers and the disbelievers, indicating the vacuity of the disbelievers’ position through a series of rhetorical questions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section cites Jonah’s repentance and complete forgiveness, warns against opponents of revelation, and affirms that the Quran or Prophet is a reminder for all.
rows.anchor: the Prophet Jonah as an example of one who repented and was forgiven in full

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators place the story in Madinah and identify its owners as three Christian or Jewish brothers in Yemen who inherited their father’s fertile garden; their father left produce for the poor, but they planned to withhold it and harvest secretly.
rows.anchor: Most commentators maintain that these verses were revealed in Madinah and that the story refers to three either Christian or Jewish brothers in Yemen

rows.speaker: Bg, IK, Z
rows.claim: “Made no exception” can mean the brothers did not say “If God wills,” showing they relied on themselves rather than God.
rows.anchor: Made no exception is taken to indicate that they did not say, “If God wills” (Bg, IK, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers’ failure to make an exception indicates self-reliance rather than trust in God.
rows.anchor: and thus trusted in themselves rather than in God (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “made no exception” can mean that they left no part of the harvest for the poor.
rows.anchor: It could also be a reference to the harvest, indicating that they left no portion for the poor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The visitation was a scourge sent by God.
rows.anchor: Visitation here indicates some form of scourge sent by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic kaʾl-ṣarīm, rendered “like a garden plucked,” can also mean “like the blackness of night.”
rows.anchor: Like a garden plucked translates kaʾl-ṣarīm, which can also mean “like the blackness of night”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly warned that disobedience can take away a servant’s sustenance, then recited this verse.
rows.anchor: The Prophet reportedly said, “Avoid sins of disobedience. Verily, the servant commits sins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers’ exclusion of the poor violated an ancient Near Eastern custom allowing the poor to glean and the Quranic command to give the harvest due on harvest day.
rows.anchor: These verses represent a violation of ancient Near Eastern custom in which the poor are allowed to glean a share of the harvest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their resolve shows their determination or overconfidence that they could control who received the produce, although only God determines.
rows.anchor: Strong in their purpose indicates that the brothers were determined or that they overestimated their own abilities

rows.speaker: IK, JJ
rows.claim: “We are astray” may mean they thought they had arrived at the wrong place or that they recognized their wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: Here we are astray indicates that they thought they had arrived at the wrong place (IK, JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their initial belief that they were astray alludes to opponents of Muhammad thinking they are guided but eventually realizing their error, as the brothers first mistake their punishment for a wrong location and then recognize it as earned.
rows.anchor: It can also be seen as an allusion to the distinction between the believers and the disbelievers mentioned in vv. 5–7

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We are deprived” recalls 56:67 and broadens the story to all harvests: God, not people, determines whether crops flourish; it may also mean “we are rendered destitute.”
rows.anchor: This verse is similar to 56:67; it reflects the broader application of this story to all manner of harvesting

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: “The most moderate” can also mean the most equitable or just among the brothers.
rows.anchor: The most moderate could also be taken to indicate the most equitable or most just among them (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brother asks why they did not thank God and attribute their blessings to Him instead of themselves.
rows.anchor: Why do you not glorify? means, “Why do you not thank God and attribute these blessings to Him rather than to yourselves?”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were wrongdoers because they prevented the poor from receiving their due.
rows.anchor: They were wrongdoers for preventing the poor from receiving their due

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The garden owners reproached each other for failing to help the poor.
rows.anchor: The owners of the garden reproached one another for their failure to help the poor (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutual blame is a torment of wrongdoers in this life and the next; Quranic wrongdoers may blame Satan, their forebears, or even God for their misguidance.
rows.anchor: Such mutual recriminations are part of the torment that afflicts wrongdoers in both this life and the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waylanā (“woe unto us”) expresses spiritual regret, often when divine punishment becomes certain; after repenting, the brothers realized God could provide better than what they made.
rows.anchor: Wayl is an exclamation of spiritual regret found elsewhere in the Quran

rows.speaker: Bg, IK, JJ
rows.claim: The brothers were reportedly given a better garden, understood either as one in this world or an allusion to the Garden in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: It is reported that they were indeed given a better garden in place of the one that they had lost (Bg, IK, JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers were punished for withholding a portion of their harvest from the poor, and disbelievers likewise face punishment for miserliness; the Hereafter’s punishment exceeds worldly disgrace.
rows.anchor: Just as the owners of the garden were punished for failing to give some portion of their harvest to the poor, so too will the disbelievers be punished for their miserliness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden’s bliss is pure and unadulterated, unlike the blessings of earthly gardens.
rows.anchor: is pure and unadulterated unlike the blessings garnered from the gardens of this world

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: When verse 34 was revealed, disbelievers reportedly boasted that their worldly favors would continue in the next life; verse 35 answered them directly.
rows.anchor: It is reported that when v. 34 was revealed, the disbelievers boasted to the Muslims that the favors they enjoyed in this world would continue in the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Maʿārij, named for the ascending ways in verse 3, belongs to the middle Makkan period.
rows.anchor: al-Maʿārij is from the middle Makkan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is also titled al-Mawāqiʿ, “Those Matters That Are Impending,” from its reference to impending punishment in verse 1, and Saʾala, “Someone Asked,” from its opening word.
rows.anchor: which is taken from the first word of the sūrah

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say the sūrah followed the preceding one immediately and continues its account of Resurrection and the Fire.
rows.anchor: Some say it was revealed immediately after the preceding sūrah and can be seen as continuing the description of the Resurrection and the Fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–7 rebuke those who mockingly ask about or seek to hasten Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: a rebuke to those who ask mockingly about or even seek to hasten the Day of Judgment (vv. 1–7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 8–18 describe Judgment Day and how it appears to those who did not believe in it or prepare for it.
rows.anchor: followed by a description of that Day and how it will appear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 19–21 are famous lines about the anxious and fretful nature of human beings.
rows.anchor: three famous verses that speak of the anxious and fretful nature of human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next passage explains how to overcome this nature by listing eight Muslim responsibilities.
rows.anchor: how one can overcome this nature, listing eight responsibilities of being a Muslim (vv. 22–35)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section describes people who reject these responsibilities and keep mocking the Prophet without understanding his message.
rows.anchor: those who reject these responsibilities and continue to deride the Prophet, having no real understanding of the message
